# The Medici, the Press, and the Capture of Meaning {#sec-1-07}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act I — The World Before California · 1300–1648
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** How does private capital come to commission public meaning —
and what happens when copying gets cheap?

**The answer.** By funding it, then staffing it, then becoming it — and the
sequence is the method. The Medici went from money changers to popes by making
themselves indispensable to the institution they wanted to control. Then the
press destroyed the information monopoly that had made such capture worth
attempting, and a century of war followed over who owned the narrative layer.

**The mechanism.** Public subsidy inverted — private capital commissioning
public meaning — and then the collapse of a chokepoint. The chapter's two halves
are the two things that can happen to a monopoly on legitimacy: it can be
bought, and it can be destroyed by a change in the cost of copying.

**The key fact.** The Medici produced four popes. A banking family did not
merely influence the institution that certified European legitimacy; it supplied
its personnel.

**The human anchor.** A commissioned altarpiece with a donor's face in it. The
most efficient statement of the mechanism in the book: the man who paid is
inside the sacred image, permanently, at eye level.

**Excluded voices.** Florentine wool workers, whose labour generated the surplus
that became the patronage; the borrowers on the other side of the ledger; and
the readers whose access to text the press expanded and whose lives the
resulting wars consumed.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that private capital converts wealth into
legitimacy by commissioning culture, and that the arrangement depends on
controlling reproduction, by showing the Medici succeed for two centuries and
then the press break the monopoly in twenty years.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Working summary

There is a Florentine altarpiece with the donor's face painted into it, at eye
level, permanently, inside the sacred image he paid for. That is the most
efficient statement of a mechanism this book will spend five acts documenting.

The Medici began as money changers and produced four popes. Their method was a
sequence: fund the institution you wish to control, then staff it, then become
it. The Medici Bank's most valuable product was not lending but the papal
accounts, and holding an institution's balance sheet makes you its constituency.
Patronage worked the same way. Leonardo, Michelangelo, and Botticelli were
commissioned, not discovered, and what the commissions bought was legitimacy.
The Renaissance, on this reading, is what happens when private capital controls
the commissioning of public meaning. Leland Stanford will build a university for
the same reason, and this book will say so again in Act II.

Then the chapter's second half destroys the thing the first half describes. The
printing press did not create literacy; it collapsed the cost of copying.
Luther's arguments in 1517 were not novel — earlier versions had been made and
their authors burned. What was new was that the theses could not be caught. An
institution whose authority rested on controlling the reproduction of text lost
that control in about twenty years.

What followed was a century of war that was not really about theology. It was
about who controlled the narrative layer of European civilisation. The Peace of
Westphalia ended it in 1648 by inventing a new unit of legitimacy: the sovereign
state. Everything after that is a fight over who controls states and whom states
protect.

The surplus that paid for the altarpieces came from Florentine wool workers, and
the wars ran through populations that had no part in starting them.

Two facts leave this chapter and both matter later: a monopoly on meaning can be
purchased, and it can be destroyed by a change in the cost of copying.
:::

::: {.chapter-question}
How does private capital come to commission public meaning — and what happens when copying gets cheap?
:::

In Florence there are altarpieces with the donor's face in them.

Not off to the side, not small, not symbolically distant — inside the sacred
scene, at eye level, kneeling among the saints, painted by the best artist
available at a cost that is a matter of surviving record. The commission bought
the man permanent placement in an image that thousands of people would look at
while thinking about eternity, in a building his family paid to complete.

It is the most efficient statement of a mechanism that this book will spend the
next four acts documenting, and it is six hundred years old.

## Funding, staffing, becoming

The Medici arrived in Florentine banking in the late fourteenth century and were
producing popes by the sixteenth. Their method, reduced to its structure, was a
sequence of three steps.

First, fund the institution you wish to control. The Medici Bank's most valuable
business was not commercial lending but the papal account — handling the
transfer of Church revenues across Europe, which was the largest single flow of
money on the continent and which required exactly the network of branches and
correspondents that the bank possessed. Holding an institution's balance sheet
does not merely make you profitable. It makes you a constituency whose interests
the institution has to consider.

Second, staff it. Church offices were an obvious placement for family members,
and the family was large and well connected. Marriages tied the Medici to other
banking houses and to the nobility. Clients and dependants accumulated across
the Florentine political system, so that the family could control the city
without holding formal office in it — Cosimo de' Medici ran Florence for thirty
years while carefully remaining a private citizen, which is the Augustan
manoeuvre from chapter 3 executed in a republic.

Third, become it. Giovanni de' Medici became Pope Leo X in 1513. Giulio de'
Medici became Clement VII in 1523. Two more Medici popes followed later in the
century. A banking family had not merely influenced the institution that
certified legitimacy across Europe. It had supplied its personnel.

## What the patronage was for

The commissions are the part everyone knows and the part most often misread.

The Medici funded Brunelleschi's dome, Donatello, Botticelli, Michelangelo, and
much else. The standard account treats this as an efflorescence of taste, and
taste was certainly involved. But cultural production in fifteenth-century
Florence was legitimacy production, and the family was in a position that
required a great deal of legitimacy: they were newly rich, they held power
without title, and they were bankers in a Church that had spent centuries
denouncing usury.

A chapel is a permanent, public, unarguable statement that the family's money is
in the service of God. A commissioned altarpiece with a donor portrait is that
statement with a name attached. Public buildings, libraries, and the sponsorship
of scholars did the same work in a secular register. This is not cynicism about
the art, which is extraordinary, or about the patrons, some of whom were
genuinely learned. It is an observation about what the transaction accomplished
for both parties.

The Renaissance, on this reading, is not a spontaneous flowering of human
creativity. It is what happens when private capital controls the commissioning
of public meaning, in a city with an unusual concentration of both.

Hold the sentence. In 1885 a railroad monopolist will convert a portion of an
extractive fortune into a university, and the university will carry his son's
name, and the transaction will be structurally identical.

## What the press did to all of this

The second half of the chapter destroys the first.

Movable type reached Europe in the middle of the fifteenth century, and its
significance was not that it created literacy — literacy was rising already —
but that it collapsed the cost of copying. A manuscript required a scribe's
labour proportional to its length, every time. A print run required a large
fixed investment and then produced copies at a marginal cost approaching the
paper.

An institution whose authority rested on controlling the reproduction and
interpretation of a small number of texts was now in a completely different
business, and it took some time to notice.

Martin Luther's ninety-five theses in 1517 are the standard marker, and the
standard account of them is wrong in an instructive way. The arguments were not
novel. Complaints about indulgences, clerical corruption, and papal authority
had circulated for well over a century. Jan Hus had made comparable arguments in
Bohemia and was burned at Constance in 1415. What was different about Luther was
not the content of the criticism but the distribution of it.

The theses were reprinted, translated, and circulated across German-speaking
Europe within weeks. Luther then wrote continuously, in German, for a popular
audience, and became by a considerable margin the best-selling author in Europe.
The Church's traditional method — identify the heretic, try him, and remove him
— had worked for centuries because it interrupted transmission. It did not work
here, because transmission was no longer running through people who could be
arrested.

## A century of war about the narrative layer

What followed was roughly a hundred and thirty years of European warfare, and
this book's interest in it is structural rather than theological.

The doctrinal questions were real and people died for them. But the war was
also, and perhaps mainly, about who would control the interpretive layer of
European civilisation now that the previous monopoly had failed — which rulers
would determine the religion of which territories, which meant which rulers
would control the schools, the courts of conscience, the marriage law, and the
legitimating apparatus of their own authority.

The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 ended the worst of it, and it ended it by
inventing something. The settlement established that the sovereign state, within
defined borders, was the basic unit of legitimacy, and that its internal
religious arrangements were not a matter for external powers. This did not
create religious freedom. It created territorial sovereignty, which is a
different and in some ways more consequential thing.

Everything after 1648 is a fight over who controls states and whom states
protect. The remainder of this book takes place inside that settlement.

## Who paid

The surplus that funded the altarpieces was generated by the Florentine wool
industry, and the workers in it had rebelled in 1378 in the Ciompi uprising,
demanding representation in a guild system that excluded them. They were
suppressed. The banking profits came in part from lending at rates that were
usurious by the Church's own doctrine, resolved through instruments designed to
be technically compliant.

And the wars ran through populations that had no part in starting them. The
Thirty Years' War killed a substantial fraction of the population of the German
lands — estimates vary widely and the range itself indicates how thoroughly the
record was destroyed — through fighting, famine, and disease.

## Two facts leaving the chapter

A monopoly on meaning can be purchased. The Medici bought one over the course of
a century, by funding an institution, staffing it, and finally occupying it.

And a monopoly on meaning can be destroyed by a change in the cost of copying.
Twenty years of cheap printing did what two centuries of dissent had not.

Both facts matter later, and they matter together. The institutions in this book
that survive longest are the ones that hold something which cannot be copied.
